Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failing test `testTooLargeFirstStep` sets up an integration scenario with an extremely short integration range (from 0.0 to 0.001) using the Dormand-Prince 8(5,3) embedded Runge-Kutta integrator. The test also forces the integrator to compute the first step size by itself by not specifying any explicit step size. The problem reported is that the integrator may compute a first step that is too large, exceeding the short integration range, and tries to evaluate the differential equation function outside the integration interval. This causes assertion failures in the test because the function is evaluated at times beyond the specified start and end limits.

The current bug report explicitly points out the root cause: the embedded Runge-Kutta integrators, such as Dormand-Prince 8(5,3), do not check or adjust their initially computed first step size to be confined within the integration range when the first step size is determined automatically by the integrator. Once this oversized step is computed, the integrator attempts to evaluate the derivatives at times beyond the range, and when it tries to backtrack, it fails to halt correctly, causing errors.

Inspecting the DormandPrince853Integrator constructor reveals it delegates to the superclass AdaptiveStepsizeIntegrator that manages step sizes and state interpolators but does not inherently limit the first step size to be within the integration bounds.

The test sets `setStepSizeControl(0, 1.0, 1.0e-6, 1.0e-8)`, but since the first step size is automatic, it can still be too large relative to the tight range of 0.001.

The absence of a step size boundary check after the first step size calculation in the relevant integration methods (likely in AdaptiveStepsizeIntegrator or DormandPrince853Integrator internals) causes this problem.

The integrators of a different family (e.g., Gragg-Bulirsch-Stoer) apparently do perform this check, avoiding this issue.

Thus, the bug occurs because the Dormand-Prince 8(5,3) integrator does not properly clamp the initial step size to the integration interval bounds when it computes the step size automatically, leading to evaluations outside the allowed integration range, which causes the test to fail.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
